text: The chaos experiments covered so far are narrow by design: one hypothesis, one injected failure. A game day is a bigger, scenario-based exercise that builds on that same safety discipline but tests something the single experiment can't — whether the team's human response holds up alongside the technical system.

A game day picks a real scenario the team believes could happen, like the primary database becoming unreachable for ten minutes, and schedules it like planned work. Two things get tested at once: the technical response — does failover actually behave the way everyone assumes — and the human response — paging, incident command, status communication, ownership. The blameless debrief afterward is usually where the real findings show up.

Here's what a game day is actually probing for: does the on-call engineer get paged correctly? Do they know they're supposed to declare an incident and pull in an incident commander, or do they quietly try to fix it alone for twenty minutes? Does the status page get updated? Does anyone remember to notify the account team before a customer does? A system that fails over flawlessly but whose team has no idea who communicates what is not actually ready for a real disaster.

This is grounded in real, documented practice. Google's SRE organization runs DiRT — Disaster Recovery Testing — deliberately scheduled exercises against real production systems and real scenarios, specifically to validate the organizational response as much as the technical one. Teams without the appetite for a full live exercise often run a lighter tabletop version instead, sometimes called a wheel of misfortune, talking through the same scenario without touching any real infrastructure.

Either version only pays off if the debrief afterward is taken as seriously as a real postmortem — writing down exactly who got paged, how long it took to declare an incident, and which runbook step turned out to be missing. Next lesson picks up exactly there: what it actually takes to turn a chaos or game-day finding into a real architecture change, instead of a write-up that gets filed away and never acted on.
